paragraphs: By the ninth stroke of Chang’an’s mourning bell, the steamers in the western market were only just being uncovered.

A flatbread seller stood in his doorway holding a bamboo tray. Someone shouted that the Grand Commandant had died, and for a long time he did not move. Steam rose past his shoulder and mingled with the morning mist. Next door the salt merchant hurried into his outer robe and asked which Grand Commandant they meant. An old soldier passing with water buckets put down his carrying pole. “Who else? Wang Jinglüe.”

Crying broke out along the avenue, though not everyone wept. Hearing Wang Meng’s name, an elderly clerk from Guanzhong first touched the corrected title deed hidden in his sleeve, then knelt facing the palace. In the doorway of a great house whose servants had once been flogged at Wang Meng’s order, men whispered about whether the officials would still investigate old accounts. While Wang Meng lived, the people of Chang’an had not always praised him. Only after his death did they realize that the man they had feared every day had himself become one of the city’s rules.

The white funeral banners had not yet all been hung in the palace. The medicine brazier in Chengming Hall was cold, but the attendants were afraid to remove it. The Heavenly King might return and order the medicine warmed again.

Empress Gou waited beyond the curtains for nearly half an hour before she heard footsteps. Fu Jian emerged ashen-faced, still wearing the robes of the night before. There were several brownish stains on his right sleeve. Usually he detested being helped to change, but now he allowed his wife to loosen his sash. The stains were blood from wiping Wang Meng’s lips. Empress Gou folded the robe, handed it to a maid, and instructed her to keep it apart.
“I only sat there for one night,” Fu Jian said.
“I know.”
“Jinglüe went quietly.”
“I know that too.”

The empress set a bowl of hot porridge before him. He looked at it, picked up his chopsticks, then put them down. They had known each other since youth and endured the most dangerous years of the Fu clan’s struggles together. She knew the shape of his hand on a sword, and knew the look he wore when he was determined not to show weakness. She offered no empty consolation. “The crown prince is waiting outside. Quan Yi has brought more than thirty documents. Lord Wang rested last night. The people of Chang’an will still need breakfast today.”
Fu Jian looked at her. Then, finally, he ate.

The Court of Imperial Sacrifices came to discuss the funeral rites. Citing ancient precedents, some officials wanted more gold and jade and a greater levy of laborers. To bury a man who had upheld the state with modest ceremony, they said, would diminish the court’s dignity. Fu Jian pushed the memorial back before he had finished reading it.

“Use the rites he prescribed while he lived. No extra gold or jade, no additional labor levy. If any prefecture demands so much as another peck of grain in the Grand Commandant’s name, write down the official responsible and bring it to me.”

The ritual official withdrew. Then Fu Jian noticed Wang Meng’s old medicine bowl at the corner of the table and realized how much his own voice had sounded like that of the dead minister. In earlier years he had often called Wang Meng too harsh when he rebuked men at court. Now there was no one left for him to complain to.

Fu Rong brought three boxes. They had been coated with tung oil, and the cords were tied in knots used by Wang Meng’s household. According to the steward, Wang Meng had sealed them himself during his illness and ordered them delivered only to the Heavenly King. In the first, Fu Jian found assessments of the court’s leading ministers. Some handwriting was darker than the rest, the notes plainly added over many years. Quan Yi, Wang Meng wrote, knew how to preserve what had been established, but needed someone beside him when a swift decision was required. Fu Rong had sound judgment, though his loyalties could make him hesitate; in danger, he could be relied on. Lü Guang was skilled in distant expeditions, but his campaigns should have definite limits. The entry on Crown Prince Fu Hong seemed to have been written especially slowly: kind-hearted and willing to ask questions, yet in need of direct experience with the clerks' work, and not to be given unchecked authority all at once.

Fu Jian turned the bamboo slip over, then turned it back again. Not one line was written to flatter the throne. He remembered Wang Meng coming to the palace at night more than a decade earlier, having somehow collected evidence of bribery among Guanzhong’s officials. He had laid roll after roll of names across Fu Jian’s knees. Fu Jian accused him of having no mercy. Wang Meng merely asked, “If Your Majesty shows them mercy today, who will show mercy to those who pay the grain tax tomorrow?”

There were far fewer names in the second box: Murong Chui, Yao Chang, Fu Chong, Fu Luo, and Murong Wei among them. Wang Meng had recorded not only the dangers they posed, but also their uses. Murong Chui was a formidable soldier, deeply attached to his lost homeland; he must not be given back his former followers. Yao Chang understood men well, and had too many old friends in the Qiang country to remain indefinitely in the palace guard. Fu Chong held fast to his veterans and to his promises; to provoke him into a sudden rupture would be folly. Fu Jian read slowly. Some judgments were familiar. Others he had spent years refusing to admit.

The third box held only a small strip of silk. There was a stain of medicine on the back, as if someone had gathered it from beside the sickbed before its author could finish. The first few lines were orderly; toward the end the strokes shook until they were scarcely legible.

“I am old and ill, and can no longer weigh the men of the realm for Your Majesty. Not all that troubles me is recorded in these boxes. Your Majesty fears leaving great affairs to those who will come after you, and would gather the work of decades into a single morning. Men in haste are easily persuaded that there must be a shorter road.”

Fu Jian rested the silk on his knees and sat for a long while. Beyond the doors, attendants hurried past with white funeral cloth. He gave the first two boxes to Fu Rong for sealing and storage at the Department of State Affairs. The strip of silk alone he folded twice and tucked into his inner sleeve.
“How much else did Lord Wang leave to say?” Fu Rong asked softly.
“Enough to occupy me for the rest of my life.”

After three days of lying in state, Wang Meng’s funeral carriage moved slowly along Vermilion Bird Avenue. His household had used no curtains threaded with gold; the white cloth covering the carriage shafts had been washed spotless, and the coffin within looked plain and heavy. Fu Jian walked behind it. Then came the imperial kinsmen, ministers, generals, and guards bearing long mourning banners. Every ward gate stood open. Children crowded the rooftops. Women scattered paper offerings toward the procession from behind the guards, and pale scraps fluttered between court boots and horses' hooves.

As the bier reached the southern market, an old woman suddenly pushed through the crowd. Soldiers of the Feathered Forest Guard lowered their halberds to stop her, but she knelt beneath the blades, holding up a pair of straw sandals. The soles had been stitched with two layers of hemp cord. They were almost worn to pieces.
“Let her through,” Fu Jian said.

Looking up at his fine robes, the woman hurried to explain. “My son’s name is Zhao Liu. The county officers took him years ago to work another man’s labor levy. He was near death on the works when Lord Wang reviewed the case and gave him his life back. Now he guards the frontier in Hedong and cannot come home. He sent these sandals by a traveler. Lord Wang, he said, used to walk the mountain paths when he was young. Perhaps he might have need of them.”

Her story was tangled, and much of what she said broke the rules of ceremony. The ritual officer came closer and hesitantly observed that only a prescribed number of objects might be placed in the coffin. Fu Jian took the sandals and felt their coarse edges, and a knot left loose on one heel.
“Place them by his feet.”

The old woman watched the bier move away, still not knowing to whom she had spoken. When the drink seller beside her told her, she was frightened and tried to kneel again. He helped her upright. “Does the Heavenly King know of Zhao Liu too?” she asked. The seller had no answer. They stood together until the procession, its white banners massed like cloud, vanished at the end of the street.

Walking among the generals, Murong Chui saw Fu Jian take the sandals himself and remembered Ye when Former Yan fell. There had been much weeping in the city that day. But once Qin’s troops entered, the cries were soon drowned beneath new military orders, grain prices, and notices of resettlement. He had thought the grief of a fallen kingdom belonged only to those who lost it. Seeing the sandals, he began to understand that the gratitude and resentment Wang Meng had earned by years of regulating officials and taxes could not be counted as easily as the possession of a city.
Someone spoke softly behind him. “General, a visitor has come from Ye.”
“Who?”
“Yue Shou.”

Murong Chui did not turn. Yue Shou, a former Yan officer, had collected the remains of fallen soldiers near Ye and, after the kingdom’s fall, worked to record the scattered names of its veterans. Such a cautious man would not have risked coming to Chang’an during the funeral merely to pay his respects.
“Tell him to enter through the small gate in the western wall at midnight. Let him speak as little as possible on the way.”

The messenger disappeared. On the other side of the bier Yao Chang also walked in the mourning procession. He happened to look up, inclined his head toward Murong Chui across the crowd, then adjusted the mourning cap that the wind had knocked askew. Neither spoke.

That night only a few lamps burned in Murong Chui’s residence. Yue Shou came through the rear door and removed the rough mourning robe he had worn over his clothes. Beneath it his frame was thin and wasted. At the sight of Murong Chui he fell to his knees and addressed him as Prince of Wu.
Murong Chui shut the door at once.
“Call me that in Chang’an again and you may not live to return to Ye tomorrow.”
Yue Shou raised his gray-haired head. “Even if Your Highness no longer acknowledges your servant, your servant still knows who you are.”
“I know who you are. Get up and tell me why you came.”

Yue Shou took an oilcloth roll from his bamboo basket and lowered his voice. The register seized at Ye had originally been a mutual-aid roll kept by the former army. After Yan fell, people from northern Ji and Hejian had been scattered across distant counties. A man seeking a living brother or his father’s burial place could travel a thousand li and still find no one to ask. Several old captains had therefore recorded households according to their former camps. Merchants contributed grain and cloth, and widows and wounded soldiers received what they needed by consulting the register. Then someone had added military markings in its margins and brought in armor whose origin no one could explain. The officials now insisted that the Yan people were gathering to rebel.
“Were there men on the register who wanted rebellion?” Murong Chui asked.
Yue Shou said nothing.
“If you came only to tell me things I would like to hear, your journey has been wasted.”

“There were,” Yue Shou admitted at last. “Some keep the old seals and have refused for ten years to call themselves Qin subjects. Some send their youngest sons into the mountains to learn riding and archery. But most of the people on that roll ... they only want millet enough to survive the winter, and to bring their lost relatives home in spring.”
“Whose armor was it?”

“I traced a wagon convoy coming from the west. The goods were unloaded in haste. The men showed a badge belonging to a certain royal household in Chang’an. The keeper of the warehouse was later found dead.”

Murong Chui asked how many wagons there had been, then how many men had accompanied Yue Shou to the capital. Seven, Yue Shou said, and all seven knew why he had come. Murong Chui’s expression darkened. In the old days, seven men defending one position were strength. Tonight seven men entrusted with a secret were seven doors through which death could enter.
“Give me the roll.”

Yue Shou hesitated, then handed it over. Murong Chui opened the oilcloth. Tiny characters crowded the pages. There were circles beside some names, measures of cloth or grain beside others; grease stained the corners. On the last sheet he found: “Sought his brother for seventeen years; has now found the burial place.” Beside it someone had hastily added: “Tell Mother.”
Murong Chui closed the roll and brought the lamp closer.
Yue Shou’s face changed. “Your Highness!”

Flame caught the corner and ran hungrily through the ink. Yue Shou lunged to save it, but Murong Chui seized his wrist and threw the remaining sheets into a bronze basin. They strained against each other until the paper had blackened to flakes. Only then did Murong Chui release him.
“Those are the lives of thousands of households,” Yue Shou said hoarsely.
“And the warrant for the deaths of thousands more.”
“Without the roll, how will they find one another?”

“You told me there were copies in Zhongshan and Hedong. Make fresh transcripts when you return. Keep the old camp lists privately for reference. The version you give to officials should record only present addresses, the whereabouts of kin, and the grain each household is owed. Do not give anyone a means to summon an army by reading a list of people searching for their families.”

Yue Shou watched the basin. Tears fell from his eyes. It was more than paper he mourned. The horsemen who had ridden beneath the Murong banners twenty years ago, the horns sounding over snowbound camps, the last Yan standard above Ye—all seemed to tremble in the fire.
“Has Your Highness truly forgotten Yan?”
“No.”
“Then why will you leave us no path back?”
“If Ye rises tomorrow, do you believe Qin’s soldiers will kill only the men carrying blades? How many children’s names were written in that book?”
Yue Shou lowered his eyes. After a long time he asked, “What if Chang’an arrests them anyway?”
“Do not bring out the swords first. I shall petition the Heavenly King for an open investigation.”
“And if he refuses?”
Murong Chui did not answer. The silence lasted so long that Yue Shou understood: the Prince of Wu had not burned every road behind him. He simply would not yet ask living men to take those roads.

By the time Yue Shou departed, cold dew had gathered in the courtyard. Murong Chui walked him to the gallery and placed the worn mourning robe in his hands. The old man put it on and disappeared into the darkness. Murong Chui returned to the lamp and began drafting recommendations for the Central Army Office. At the words “former Yan households shall no longer be grouped by their old units,” his brush paused. He set the paper beneath his inkstone. He had been too quick with the fire tonight. He still had to decide whether he would dare tell the court tomorrow what he had done.

On the day before Wang Meng’s burial, Yao Chang visited Fu Chong’s residence with a jar of wine to offer condolences. The old general had said he was ill and would receive no guests. But on learning who had come, he ordered the side gate opened.

Most of the weapons had been removed from the rack in the main hall. Fu Chong’s old saddle still hung beneath the gallery, its bronze rings polished bright. Yao Chang removed his cloak and poured two bowls of wine, placing one before Wang Meng’s memorial portrait and passing the other to Fu Chong.
“Wang Jinglüe did not like you,” Fu Chong said.
“I cannot say he was fond of the general either.”
Fu Chong snorted, but accepted the bowl.

Yao Chang drank slowly. He recalled earlier campaigns, nights when Qiang soldiers slept on the river flats and the supply wagons failed to arrive, and Fu Chong shared out a cart of coarse bran cakes. Back then a man did not ask whether a hungry soldier was Di or Qiang. Whoever had grain fed the others. Fu Chong’s expression softened as he listened. Then Yao Chang spoke of the tiger tallies being taken away, of grain allocations now requiring signatures from several offices, of old generals unable to give two wounded men an extra reward without petitioning for approval.
“Whom will the men obey now?” Yao Chang asked.
“Whom?” Anger flashed in Fu Chong’s eyes. “The court. Is that not what the Heavenly King himself ordered?”

“Indeed.” Yao Chang lifted his empty bowl. “The virtue of court government is that many hands share the work. Its failing is that many hands share it. A veteran comes crying to your door in poverty, and you reach for a grain sack that is no longer there. But he still remembers the days when you had one.”

Fu Chong could find no reply. Yao Chang turned the conversation to the price of horses, as though the previous exchange had been idle talk. At the door Fu Chong suddenly asked about the royal-household badge rumored to have appeared at Ye. Yao Chang displayed exactly the right degree of surprise. He had lived in Chang’an so long, he said, that he knew no more than anyone else. Best that Fu Chong send men to investigate promptly, lest he be implicated through no fault of his own.

Outside the gate Yao Chang passed a guardsman of the Fu household wearing a narrow leather belt. The man’s right hand touched his waist in a quick, almost invisible gesture. Yao Chang did not slow or look back. His servant saw no change in his expression. Only once they had turned out of the lane did he dare whisper that news had arrived last night: a rider had left the Fu residence by the rear gate and taken the old road to Xianyang.

Yao Chang lifted the carriage curtain and looked out upon the city’s white mourning banners. He did not know whether that rider was bound for the Qiang country or Hebei, much less who had sent him. But he remembered Fu Chong’s trembling hand around the wine bowl, and Murong Chui’s glance down the street during the funeral procession. If an hour came when those things mattered, the hidden thoughts of these men might prove worth more than the soldiers they commanded.

A high wind swept the country outside Chang’an on the day Wang Meng was buried. A plain stone monument stood before the new mound. Fu Jian helped bear the funeral cord and watched the coffin lowered into the earth. At first, each shovelful struck the wood with a muffled thud. As the earth rose, the sound grew fainter and disappeared. Fu Hong stood behind his father. He had held the army’s provision ledgers through a whole night in the Department of State Affairs and had seen Wang Meng chastise officers at court. Now he did not know what to do with his hands.

Fu Jian gave him a spray of white flowers to place before the grave. Fu Hong crouched and saw broken grass mixed with the wet soil. “If I make mistakes in the years ahead,” he said suddenly, “Lord Wang will no longer be here to scold me.”
“There are many others at court who will scold you,” Fu Jian answered softly. “See first that they are not afraid to do so.”

When the rites were over, Fu Rong came from behind the mourners and spoke quietly at Fu Jian’s side. Fu Liang, a guard who had left Fu Chong’s residence, had vanished on the old Xianyang road. Marks of a change of horses remained at a crossing, and his family had already departed the capital. A former Yan officer had also visited Murong Chui the night before, carrying a bamboo basket when he arrived and leaving with empty hands.
Fu Jian looked at the still-wet grave. “None of them has been idle.”
“Elder Brother, shall I question Murong Chui first?”
“Question him tonight and he will give me an excellent answer. Wait. Find out where his visitor went.”

Fu Rong was about to assent when hooves thundered up the mountain road. A rider burst through the mourners and nearly fell with his horse at the foot of the slope. He was gasping too hard to speak a complete sentence. All he could do was hold up a dispatch marked with an emergency seal.

The armory at Ye had burned. Its captain had been found dead in a well outside the city. The weapons and armor once hidden in the storehouse had been carried off during the fire, and the register that had cast suspicion on every Yan household in the city had vanished as well.

Fu Jian opened the dispatch and read it twice. The mountain wind lifted his sleeve, pressing Wang Meng’s strip of silk against his wrist. He neither glanced toward Murong Chui among the generals nor summoned Fu Chong. He called only for Fu Rong.

“Take officers from the Court of Justice and the registry administration to Ye. Begin with the warehouse, the wagons, and the missing roll. If a man is suspected, find evidence. If anyone uses rumor as a warrant for arrests, first ask who gave him the courage to do it.”
“I shall leave at once.”

Fu Rong rode down the mountain as the mourners began making their slow way back toward the city. The road was churned with wheel tracks. The sky remained pale and gray, and women still wept as they walked. Fu Jian lingered until the last of the elderly ministers had gone. Then he crouched beside the monument and secured a corner of white cloth that the wind had lifted from the grave.

When he rose, the clouds had begun to part in the east. The new earth was no different from the old mountain soil. Only the two carved characters of Wang Meng’s name still carried white dust from the mason’s chisel. Fu Jian withdrew his hand from the stone and mounted his horse.
At the far end of the official road, Fu Rong’s riders had already raised the first plume of dust.
